description: Dual-process theory proposes that human cognition operates via two fundamentally different systems: a fast, automatic, intuitive system and a slow, deliberate, analytical system. This framework is central to understanding when and why critical thinking fails — and why the mere capacity to think critically doesn't guarantee that it will be used.
dewey_connection: Dewey's description of the distinction between 'immediate experience' and 'reflective thinking' anticipates the System 1/System 2 distinction. Dewey noted that most thinking is associative and habit-driven; genuine reflection requires interrupting automatic response patterns. System 2 engagement corresponds to Dewey's five phases of reflective inquiry.
paul_elder_connection: Paul and Elder's Intellectual Virtues are essentially System 2 dispositions — intellectual humility, for example, requires override of System 1's egocentric default. The Standards function as System 2 quality criteria that must be deliberately applied.

system_1.name: System 1

core_characteristics.capacity: High — can process multiple inputs simultaneously
core_characteristics.evolution: Evolutionarily older; shared with other animals

what_it_does: Rapid causal attribution ('he slipped because the floor was wet')
Retrieval of associated memories, feelings, and stereotypes
critical_thinking_risks: Produces answers that feel certain but may be wrong
Subject to heuristic biases — availability, representativeness, anchoring
Egocentric and socioentric defaults — sees one's own view as obvious
Motivated reasoning — selectively processes information that confirms existing beliefs
First-impression anchoring — initial impressions disproportionately shape subsequent evaluation

system_2.name: System 2

core_characteristics.control: Subject to intentional direction and interruption
core_characteristics.evolution: Evolutionarily newer; more prominent in humans

what_it_does: Self-reflective cognition — thinking about one's thinking
critical_thinking_opportunities: Can override System 1 defaults when engaged
Can apply explicit standards to evaluate implicit impressions
Can generate and systematically evaluate multiple alternatives
Can recognize and compensate for known biases
Enables metacognitive monitoring of one's own reasoning processes
limitations: Depletes with use — cognitive resource exhaustion
Often fails to engage even when needed — default acceptance of System 1 outputs
Can rationalize System 1 conclusions post-hoc rather than evaluate them genuinely
Slower is not necessarily more accurate — can be wrong in different ways

dimensions.system_1: Recognizing a friend's face; feeling disgust; 2+2=4
dimensions.system_2: Planning a budget; evaluating a novel argument; learning a new procedure

stanovich_tripartite_model.description: Stanovich and West (2000) proposed a refinement of the two-system model into three levels, providing a more fine-grained account of why smart people make systematic reasoning errors.

levels.abbreviation: TASS = The Autonomous Set of Systems
levels.description: Fast, encapsulated processes that operate automatically. Cannot be directly overridden by intention — can only be inhibited or checked.
levels.key_insight: TASS outputs feel like perceptions — they arrive as intuitions, impressions, or feelings, not as conclusions of reasoning.

levels.description: The processing efficiency of slow, deliberate cognition. Measured by traditional IQ and working memory tests. Represents the computational horsepower for deliberate reasoning.
levels.key_insight: Having a high-capacity algorithmic mind does not guarantee good reasoning — it only provides the resource for good reasoning. How those resources are directed is determined by the reflective mind.

levels.corresponds_to: The meta-level of System 2 — what decides when and how to engage the algorithmic mind
levels.description: The disposition and values system that determines whether and how cognitive resources are deployed. Encompasses epistemic values: belief in rationality, concern for truth, intellectual virtues.
levels.key_insight: Stanovich argues that many reasoning errors are failures of the reflective mind, not the algorithmic mind. Intelligent people often reason poorly because their reflective mind does not value rational scrutiny — or directs their algorithmic power toward motivated reasoning rather than truth-seeking.

stanovich_tripartite_model.ct_implication: Critical thinking development must address all three levels: automatizing some basic skills (TASS), building processing capacity (Algorithmic), and — most importantly — cultivating the epistemic values and metacognitive dispositions that govern when and how cognitive resources are deployed (Reflective).

cognitive_biases.description: Systematic errors in thinking that arise primarily from System 1 defaults. Understanding biases enables System 2 counter-strategies.

biases.mechanism: Selectively seeking, interpreting, and remembering information that confirms existing beliefs
biases.example: A researcher reads only studies that support their preferred hypothesis
biases.ct_counter_strategy: Actively seek disconfirming evidence; steel-man opposing positions; ask 'what would change my mind?'

biases.mechanism: Judging the probability or frequency of events by how easily examples come to mind
biases.example: Overestimating the frequency of plane crashes because they are vividly reported in media
biases.ct_counter_strategy: Seek base rates and statistical evidence; distinguish memorability from frequency

biases.mechanism: Disproportionate reliance on the first piece of information encountered when making judgments
biases.example: Negotiators who hear a high initial offer make higher final offers than those who hear a low initial offer
biases.ct_counter_strategy: Deliberately generate your own estimate before encountering anchors; consider multiple reference points

biases.mechanism: Systematic overestimation of one's own knowledge, ability, and the accuracy of one's judgments
biases.example: People rate their driving skills or knowledge accuracy well above average across all groups
biases.ct_counter_strategy: Track prediction accuracy over time; explicitly consider how you might be wrong; seek calibration feedback

biases.mechanism: Judging the probability that something belongs to a category by how similar it is to the prototype of that category, ignoring base rates
biases.example: A quiet, book-reading person is assumed more likely to be a librarian than a farmer — ignoring that farmers are far more numerous
biases.ct_counter_strategy: Explicitly consider base rates; ask 'what is the prior probability here?'

biases.mechanism: Continuing to invest resources in a failing course of action because of prior investment (irretrievable costs)
biases.example: Staying in an unhappy relationship because 'I've already invested so much time'
biases.ct_counter_strategy: Evaluate future options based on future costs and benefits, not past investment; ask 'if I were starting fresh today, would I choose this?'

biases.mechanism: People with low competence in a domain tend to overestimate their own performance, partly because they lack the metacognitive skill to recognize their deficiencies
biases.example: A beginning student rates their essay as excellent because they cannot yet recognize its weaknesses
biases.ct_counter_strategy: Seek expert feedback; study domain competence standards explicitly; track performance empirically

biases.mechanism: Evaluating information, arguments, and people more favorably when they are associated with one's own social group
biases.example: Accepting weak arguments from politicians one supports while demanding strong evidence from opponents
biases.ct_counter_strategy: Apply consistent standards across in-group and out-group claims; test whether one would accept equivalent arguments from the other side

crt_example.name: Cognitive Reflection Test (CRT)
crt_example.author: Shane Frederick, 2005
crt_example.description: A three-item test designed to measure the tendency to override an incorrect intuitive response with a correct deliberate one. High CRT scorers are better at System 2 engagement.

classic_item.question: A bat and a ball cost $1.10 in total. The bat costs $1.00 more than the ball. How much does the ball cost?
classic_item.correct_answer: $0.05 (requires System 2 to override intuition and check the math)
classic_item.why_hard: System 1 immediately suggests '10 cents' by decomposing 1.10 into 1.00 + 0.10. System 2 must notice this is wrong: if ball=$0.10 and bat costs $1.00 more, bat=$1.10, total=$1.20 ≠ $1.10.

app_usage.concept_feature: Explain System 1/System 2 in Concept Explorer as foundational metacognitive knowledge
app_usage.bias_library: 8 biases with examples and counter-strategies — surfaced when reviewing reasoning
app_usage.exercise_feature: CRT-style exercises that require System 2 override
app_usage.template_feature: Bias self-check as a template component in the Dewey Reflective Template
app_usage.llm_integration: Claude can identify System 1 patterns in user reasoning and flag likely biases
